Abstract
19
Studying C functional group distributions in decomposing litterfall samples is one of the
20
common methods of studying litterfall decomposition processes. However, the methods of
21
studying the C functional group distributions, such as 13C-NMR spectroscopy, are expensive
22
and time consuming and new rapid and inexpensive technologies should be sought. Therefore,
23
this study examined whether laboratory-based hyperspectral image analysis can be used to
24
predict C functional group distributions in decomposing litterfall samples. Hyperspectral
25
images were captured from ground decomposing litterfall samples in the visible to near infrared
26
(VNIR) spectral range of 400-1000 nm. Partial least-square regression (PLSR) and artificial
27

2

neural network (ANN) models were used to correlate the VNIR reflectance data measured from
28
the litterfall samples with their C functional group distributions determined using 13C-NMR
29
spectroscopy. The results showed that alkyl-C, O,N-alkyl-C, di-O-alkyl-C1, di-O-alkyl-C2,
30
aryl-C1, aryl-C2 and carboxyl derivatives could be acceptably predicted using the PLSR model,
31
with R2 values of 0.72, 0.73, 0.71, 0.74, 0.76, 0.75 and 0.63 and ratio of prediction to deviation
32
(RPD) values of 1.86, 1.82, 1.78, 1.71, 1.90, 1.76 and 1.43, respectively. Predicted O,N-alkyl-
33
C, di-O-alkyl-C1, di-O-alkyl-C2, aryl-C1 and aryl-C2 using the ANN model provided R2 values
34
of 0.62, 0.68, 0.69, 0.82 and 0.67 and the RPDs of 1.54, 1.76, 1.52, 2.10 and 1.72, respectively.
35
With the exception of aryl-C1, the PLSR model was more reliable than the ANN model for
36
predicting C functional group distributions given limited amount of training data. Neither the
37
PLSR nor the ANN model could predict the carbohydrate-C and O-aryl-C acceptably. Overall,
38
laboratory-based hyperspectral imaging in combination with the PLSR modelling can be
39
recommended for the analysis of C functional group distribution in the decomposing forest
40
litterfall samples.
41
1 Introduction
42
Litterfall decomposition is an ecological process affecting carbon (C) and nutrient cycling in
43
forest ecosystems (Swift et al., 1979; Trumbore and Czimczik, 2008; Wang et al., 2015).
44
Litterfall decomposition improves soil quality through the addition of organic matter enhancing
45
soil physicochemical properties such as soil water holding capacity and filtration, soil
46
biodiversity and soil microorganism activity (Bossa et al., 2005; Ngoran et al., 2006; Wang et
47
al., 2015). Litterfall decomposition rate is considered to be influenced by different factors such
48
as litterfall quality, which can be investigated through analysing litterfall C functional groups
49
(Bejarano et al., 2014; Bonanomi et al., 2013; Finn et al., 2015; Knorr et al., 2005; Xiao et al.,
50
2013). Significant correlations have been reported among litterfall C functional groups
51

3

including alkyl-C, N-alkyl-C, O-alkyl-C, di-O-alkyl-C and litterfall decomposition rate
52
(Bonanomi et al., 2013). Studying the C functional groups in decomposing litterfall is therefore
53
relevant to studies addressing C and nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems.
54
Solid-state 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (13C-NMR) spectroscopy has been used
55
successfully to examine the C cycling and to study the effects of litterfall quality on
56
decomposition processes (Almendros et al., 2000; Baldock et al., 2004; Bell‐Dereske et al.,
57
2016; Incerti et al., 2017; Mathers et al., 2007). However, 13C-NMR spectroscopy is an
58
expensive and time-consuming technique for studying large numbers of samples. Therefore, it
59
is important to develop complementary, rapid, inexpensive and reliable technologies for the
60
study of decomposing litterfall quality.
61
Hyperspectral imaging, which utilises the advantages of both conventional imaging and
62
spectroscopy in a single instrument, has emerged as one of the most promising methods for
63
rapid, facile and non-destructive evaluation of diverse materials (Elmasry et al., 2012; Manley,
64
2014). Hyperspectral imaging systems use a wide range of electromagnetic spectra, from
65
ultraviolet to infrared, to acquire information on both the spatial and the spectral distribution
66
of the materials (Elmasry et al., 2012; Koehler et al., 2002; Manley, 2014). Hyperspectral
67
reflectance values are correlated with reference values using multivariate analyses, such as
68
linear and non-linear regression models (Kamruzzaman et al., 2015; Manley, 2014;
69
Tahmasbian et al., 2017). Dimensionality reduction or feature selection (band selection)
70
techniques, such as principal component analyses (PCA), stepwise feature selection and
71
particle swarm optimisation (PSO), are usually employed prior to multivariate analyses. This
72
is due to the high dimensionality of the hyperspectral data, with many non-informative bands
73
(Cen et al., 2016; Fenzández et al., 2016; Naganathan et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2017; Yang et al.,
74
2007).
75

4

After selecting the most important bands by using an appropriate band selection technique, the
76
raw data can then be subjected to multivariate analyses directly. However, transformation of
77
spectral data is often required to reduce the impact of artefacts, such as light scattering, random
78
noise, and baseline shift effects (Kamruzzaman et al., 2015; Manley, 2014; Tahmasbian et al.,
79
2017). The most common data transformation methods include first and second derivatives,
80
normalization and scaling, multiplicative scatter correction (MSC), standard normal variate
81
(SNV) and orthogonal signal correction (OSC) (Fearn, 2000; Kamruzzaman et al., 2016;
82
Rinnan et al., 2009; Siripatrawan et al., 2011; Tahmasbian et al., 2017). The transformed data
83
are then used to develop the multivariate model. This step employs appropriate chemometric
84
algorithms, such as partial least squares regression (PLSR) and artificial neural network
85
(ANN), as linear and non-linear calibration methods, respectively (Balabin et al., 2011; Guo et
86
al., 2016; Kuang et al., 2015a).
87
The PLSR model has been used, as linear regression algorithms, in chemometrics for a variety
88
of subjects (Antonucci et al., 2010; Higashikawa et al., 2014; Kamruzzaman et al., 2016;
89
Tahmasbian et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2016). Unlike multiple linear regression, PLSR can analyse
90
data which are strongly correlated with multiple variables (Höskuldsson, 1988; Wold et al.,
91
1984; Wold et al., 2001). The PLSR model performs well with noisy and small datasets and
92
chooses the response variable by generating independent latent variables (LV) from the
93
strongest prediction of cross-validation (Höskuldsson, 1988; Pirouz, 2006; Wold et al., 1984;
94
Wold et al., 2001). The ANN model, inspired by the animal brain, is a powerful machine
95
learning algorithm and intelligent prediction tool used in chemometrics (Balabin et al., 2011;
96
Guo et al., 2016; Larose and Larose, 2014). The ANN model can work well when using noisy
97
and uninformative datasets, as it assigns weights to each artificial neurone connection (Larose
98
and Larose, 2014).
99

5

Hyperspectral imaging technology has been used to study a diverse range of systems, including
100
medical and pharmaceutical systems, forest ecosystems and food and agricultural products
101
(Kamruzzaman et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2015; Gama et al., 2018; Song et al., 2012; Sytar et al.,
102
2017; Tahmasbian et al., 2017). To the best of our knowledge, however, this is the first paper
103
studying the possibility of using a laboratory-based hyperspectral image analysis and
104
multivariate regression models to predict C functional group distribution in decomposing
105
litterfall samples.
106
2 Methods and materials
107
2.1
Study site description
108
The decomposing litterfall samples used in the current experiment were taken from a litterfall
109
decomposition experiment conducted in Toohey Forest, a suburban native forest located in
110
south-eastern Queensland, Australia (27°32′S, 153°03′E) (Fig. 1). Toohey Forest covers an
111
area of about 681 ha. The forest contains 460 species of vascular plants dominated by different
112
species of eucalypt (Butler et al., 2016; Catterall and Wallace, 1987; Catterall et al., 2001;
113
Farmer et al., 2004). The climate of the region is subtropical, with average minimum
114
temperature (1939-2016) of 14.4 °C, average maximum temperature (1939-2016) of 26.3 °C
115
and mean annual precipitation (1969-2016) of 1163.5 mm. Prescribed burning has been applied
116
in Toohey Forest since 1993 with different intervals for different sites (Butler et al., 2016;
117
Catterall et al., 2001; Tahmasbian et al., 2017).
118
2.2
Experimental design, sample collection and preparation
119
A total of 118 decomposing litterfall samples were collected from three different study sites
120
covering 6000 m2, within a 15-month period starting in August 2012. Litterfall samples from
121
Site 1 (27° 32' 26.79'' S, 153° 02' 39.81'' E) were collected monthly in the first six-months and
122

6

then seasonally (every three months) for the next nine months. Litterfall samples were collected
123
seasonally from Site 2 (27° 32'47.33"S, 153° 3'8.55"E) and Site 3 (27° 32' 28.61'' S, 153° 02'
124
50.60'' E). Sites 1, 2 and 3, were subjected to prescribed burning in 2011, 2008, and 2006,
125
respectively.
126
The microplot experimental method, employing complete randomised block design, was used
127
for the litterfall decomposition experiment (Blumfield et al., 2004; Xu et al., 1993b; Xu et al.,
128
1993a) (Fig. 2). The litterfall samples were carefully removed by hand from the microplots and
129
stored in paper bags prior to C functional group analysis using solid state 13C NMR
130
spectroscopy. The samples were then stored in sterile polyethylene vial tubes at room
131
temperature for subsequent analyses using a laboratory-based hyperspectral imaging system.
132
2.3
13C NMR spectroscopy
133
Solid-state 13C CPMAS NMR spectroscopy was used to characterise the changes in the C
134
functional group distributions in the leaf litterfall samples during the decomposition process.
135
Ground litterfall samples were packed in a 7 mm diameter silicon nitride rotor and spun at 5
136
kHz at the magic angle. The cross-polarization sequence tancpx, contained within the VnmrJ
137
3.1A software package, was used with the contact time of 1.2 ms, the 20 ms of acquisition time
138
and 2.5 s of recycle delay. A total 2000 transients were collected for litterfall samples with a
139
sweep width of 36 kHz. The peak area of 9 chemical shift regions (C functional groups) was
140
measured using the MestreNova software (Table 1). To facilitate compensation for spinning
141
side bands intensity, integrals were calculated using narrow spectral intervals when required.
142
The NMR analyses were conducted using a 300 MHz Varian VNMRS spectrometer (Varian
143
Inc., CA) operated at a frequency of 75.4 MHz.
144

7

2.4
Hyperspectral imaging system and image acquisition
145
A laboratory-based visible-near infrared (VNIR) hyperspectral imaging system, located in the
146
Plant Ecology Laboratory at University of the Sunshine Coast and operated in the spectral
147
range of 400-1000 nm, was used in this experiment. The system consisted of a 12-bit line
148
scanner camera (Pika XC2, USA) with a spectral resolution of 1.3 nm (producing a total of 462
149
spectral bands); a 23 mm of focal length lens; a linear translation stage operated by a stepper
150
motor; four current-controlled wide spectrum quartz halogen lights and data acquisition
151
software (SpectrononPro 2.94, Resonon, USA).
152
Approximately 7 g of the ground decomposing litterfall samples were put in plastic weigh-
153
trays and placed on the translation stage, then moved into the camera’s field of view. The speed
154
of translation stage and the exposure time were set at 1.23 mm sec-1 and the 27.31 ms,
155
respectively. After capturing each image, the samples were homogenised, by manual shaking.
156
Sample homogenization and image capture were repeated until reproducible spectral signatures
157
were obtained for consecutive images (Tahmasbian et al., 2017).
158
2.5
Spectral profile extraction and data calibration
159
Images (2 × 2 cm) were cropped from the background and the corrected average reflectance
160
(R) of the samples extracted using the SpectrononPro software package (version 2.94, Resonon,
161
USA). Image correction was conducted by removing the average dark current noise (dark
162
calibration) and the response correction (white calibration) by the SpectrononPro software
163
during the image acquisition. Response spectra was represented in supplementary material
164
(Fig. S1). Dark correction was applied, by capturing the image with the lights off and the lens
165
cap on, prior to capturing images from samples. White correction was applied by capturing the
166
reflectance of a white Teflon sheet (Resonon, USA) providing approximately 99 % of
167

8

reflectance. The R was then calculated from the uncorrected spectral reflectance (R0) using Eq.
168

2.6
Data pre-processing
173
2.6.1 Outlier detection and data division
174
Outliers should be detected and removed from dataset to establish a reliable robust model
175
(Morellos et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2014; Tahmasbian et al., 2017). Outliers may be caused by
176
instrumental errors, operational errors, fluctuations in work environment and any significant
177
difference in the sample matrix (Li and Qu, 2016; Liu et al., 2008).
178
In this experiment, principal-component-analyses (PCA) were performed to identify the
179
outliers using the Hotelling’s T2 test within 99 % of confidence level (Jiang et al., 2016; Li and
180
Qu, 2016; Morellos et al., 2016; Tahmasbian et al., 2017). The identified outliers were
181
removed from the dataset and the remaining data, for each C functional group, were randomly
182
divided into a calibration set and a test set. Approximately 80% and 20% of the data were
183
assigned to the calibration and test sets, respectively (Kohavi, 1995; Tahmasbian et al., 2017).
184
A t-test was carried out to compare both sets, to confirm consistent coverage of the whole range
185
of values for each C functional group (Barbin et al., 2012; Tahmasbian et al., 2017).
186
The descriptive analyses of C functional group distributions of the decomposing litterfall
187
samples determined by 13C NMR spectroscopy have been summarised in Table 1. The
188

9

maximum and minimum values were observed for Alk and diOAlk2, respectively. According
189
to the t-test results, the averages of the calibration data and those of the test data were not
190
statistically different at p<0.05.
191
2.6.2 Band selection
192
The large number of bands (n = 462) produced by the camera in this experiment were subjected
193
to band selection prior to conducting the multivariate analysis. Band selection reduces the
194
problem size and results in the reduction in search space for the needed learning algorithm,
195
thus simplifying the calculations. The process selected a subset of bands, which formed
196
patterns, from the original set of bands in the dataset (Wang et al., 2007). The selected subset
197
should contain the most necessary bands and be sufficient to describe target concepts, while
198
maintaining a suitably high accuracy in the representation of the original features (Wang et al.,
199
2007). In the current experiment, the particle swarm optimisation (PSO) technique was used to
200
select the most informative bands, from the 462 bands acquired. The PSO, inspired by the
201
simulation of the simplified social behaviour of bird flocking, is one of the most trusted feature
202
selection techniques developed by Kennedy and Eberhart (Kennedy and Eberhart, 1995a;
203
Kennedy and Eberhart, 1995b). The PSO considered each potential solution as a particle with
204
a certain velocity and ‘flies’ through the problem space. The particles adjusted their flight
205
according to their own flying experience and their companions’ flying experience, finding the
206
optimal region of complex search spaces through the interaction of individuals within a
207
population of particles. The PSO band selection was conducted using the Weka software
208
package (version 3.8.0, Hamilton, New Zealand) (Qi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2007).
209
2.6.3 Data transformation
210
Several transformation techniques, such as de-trending, first and second derivatives,
211
multiplicative scatter correction (MSC), standard normal variate (SNV) and orthogonal signal
212

10

correction (OSC), were performed on the PSO selected bands of calibration data, to remove
213
the influence of undesired effects (Fearn, 2000; Kamruzzaman et al., 2016; Rinnan et al., 2009;
214
Tahmasbian et al., 2017). All computations for outlier detection and data transformation were
215
performed using the Unscrambler® X software package (version10.4, CAMO Software Inc.,
216
Trondheim, Norway).

Model development and evaluation
218
PLSR and ANN models were developed to correlate the values of each C functional group
219
distribution in decomposing litterfall samples with the corresponding reflectance in the PSO
220

221

2.7.2 ANN model
245
A feed-forward multilayer perceptron neural network, with a Levenberg-Marquardt (LM)
246

247

248

249

250

251

252

2.7.3 Cross-validation
266
To avoid over-fitting and to select the optimum LV and NN in PLSR and ANN, a k-fold (k =
267
10) cross-validation method was used, as this was one of the most common and reliable cross-
268
validation techniques (Kohavi, 1995). In the k-fold cross-validation, the data were split, almost
269
equally, into k sets. The model was developed with (k – 1) sets, with one set left out for
270
validation. In the next iteration, a different set was left out for the validation and process
271
continues until each set was left out of the model once (Afandi et al., 2016; Balabin et al., 2011;
272
Baumann, 2003; Forina et al., 2004; Parsons et al., 2011).

3 Results and Discussion
288
3.1
Model development using the calibration datasets
289
The best fitted PLSR and ANN models were selected with the highest R2c and R2cv and lowest
290
RMSEc and RMSEcv (Table 2). Both fitted PLSR and ANN models provided acceptable
291
correlations (R2c ≥ 0.60) in the calibration set between the C functional group distributions, as
292
predicted from the hyperspectral reflectance data and as observed in the 13C NMR experiments.
293
In cross-validation sets, PLSR provided acceptable correlation (R2cv ≥ 0.60) between C
294
functional group distributions and their corresponding hyperspectral reflectance data, with the
295
exception of OAryl. The ANN also provided R2cv of greater than 0.60 in cross-validation sets,
296
with the exception of Alk and OAryl. The details are provided in the following sections.
297
3.1.1 Data pre-processing
298
Eleven samples were removed from the raw data by Hotelling’s T2 test. The remaining 107
299
samples were divided randomly into the calibration sets with approximately 80 % of samples
300
(86 samples) and test sets with approximately 20 % of samples (21 samples) (Kohavi, 1995;
301
Tahmasbian et al., 2017). Only the PSO selected bands were used for model development
302
(Daamouche and Melgani, 2009; Su et al., 2014). Table 2 shows the number of PSO selected
303
bands for each C functional group. The raw spectral calibration data, as well as the transformed
304
spectral data, were used to develop PLSR and ANN models. The results showed that all the
305
best PLSR and ANN models were developed from the data subjected to the transformation.
306
The most efficient data transformation techniques used to develop PLSR and ANN models for
307
each C functional group are summarised in Table 2. Transformation of data has been also used
308
by other studies employing hyperspectral image analysis (Fearn, 2000; Fearn et al., 2009;
309
Kamruzzaman et al., 2016; Tahmasbian et al., 2017).
310

15

3.1.2 PLSR model characteristics
311
The best PLSR models for all C functional groups were developed where the data were OSC-
312
transformed, either alone or in combination with MSC. The OSC algorithm performed by
313
finding directions in X factors that described large amounts of variance while being orthogonal
314
to Y and subtracting them from the X matrix (Fearn, 2000; Wold et al., 1998). By applying
315
MSC, each individual spectrum was regressed to the average of the all spectra by partial least
316
squares. The offset value was then subtracted and each band was divided over the slope (Agelet
317
and Hurburgh Jr, 2010; Fearn et al., 2009).
318
One of the most critical steps in developing PLSR model was selecting the correct LV. Each
319
investigated system was assumed to be influenced by a few LVs rather than all possible X
320
variables (Wold et al., 2001). More LVs led to an over-fitted model with the poor prediction
321
ability. Too few LVs might result in under-fitting; hence, the model would not be able to
322
capture the variation of the data (Abdi, 2010). The optimal LVs of the PLSR models predicting
323
C functional groups were selected at the lowest values of PRESS obtained (Abdi, 2010;
324
Kamruzzaman et al., 2016; Tahmasbian et al., 2017). The values of LVs were represented in
325
Table 2 (Details are illustrated in the supplementary material Fig. S2).
326
The results showed that only one LV was selected for most of the C functional groups. The
327
LV was one, most probably, because there was a single dependent variable (Y) and the
328
independent variables (PSO selected X variables) were not intercorrelated, or in other words,
329
XT X was diagonal (Wold et al., 2001). Therefore, one LV might show that the PLSR arrived
330
at multiple linear solution in the first component (Wold et al., 2001).

3.1.3 ANN model characteristics
332
For the majority of C functional groups, the best ANN models were developed using OSC
333
transformed data in combination with MSC and SNV. The SNV resulted in the best
334
performance for modelling of the Aryl2. The SNV removed multiplicative interference of
335
scatter and particle size by mean centring the data and then scaling them with the standard
336
deviation of each spectrum (Barnes et al., 1989; Rinnan et al., 2009). First derivative resulted
337
in the best performance for modelling of the diOAlk1 and OAryl. The first derivative removed
338
the baseline from the spectra, in addition to removing multiplicative interference from scatter
339
and particle size (Manley, 2014; Rinnan et al., 2009; Wu et al., 1995).
340
Selecting the appropriate NN in hidden layer was important to achieve a robust fit when using
341
an ANN model development technique (Larose, 2006; Larose and Larose, 2014). Many
342
methods have been proposed to define the optimal NN, however, most of the studies have
343
chosen the NN based on trial and error (Afandi et al., 2016; Dou et al., 2005; Kuang et al.,
344
2015b; Maftoonazad et al., 2011). The selected NNs in the current experiment varied between
345
six and twenty four for different C functional groups (Table 2) (Details are provided in the
346
supplementary material, Fig. S3).
347
3.1.4 Models attributes
348
The developed PLSR and ANN models performed well (R2cv > 0.60) for predicting of most of
349
the C functional group distributions in the calibration and cross-validation sets (Table 2). The
350
models were best fitted to Aryl1 with R2cv of 0.86 and 0.88, respectively for PLSR and ANN.
351
The PLSR and ANN models were poorly fitted to OAryl with R2cv of 0.58 and 0.54,
352
respectively (Table 2). Despite the different R2c for Aryl1 and OAryl regarding PLSR models
353
and different R2cv regarding ANN, the RMSEc and RMSEcv were equal for Aryl1 and OAryl
354
regarding PLSR and ANN, respectively (Table 2). The possible explanation was that, unlike
355

17

R2, RMSE was not a scaled index and might not be comparable for different (or differently
356
transformed) data.
357
The selected PLSR and ANN models developed using calibration data were then evaluated
358
using test dataset.
359
3.2
Model evaluation using the test datasets
360
For the majority of C functional groups, the values predicted from the hyperspectral data using
361
the developed PLSR and ANN models correlated well with the corresponding data obtained
362
from 13C NMR experiments in the external test sets (Fig. 4–6). With the exception of the Aryl1
363
region, PLSR predicted the C functional groups more accurately than ANN. Neither PLSR nor
364
ANN models predicted OAryl and Carb regions successfully (Fig. 7).
365
The result of testing the models showed that the best predictions of both PLSR and ANN were
366
obtained for Aryl1. The PLSR reliably predicted Aryl1 in the test samples with the RPD of 1.90
367
(Fig. 4a). A regression model was considered ‘reliable’ where the RPD calculated for
368
prediction was above 1.4 (Bellon-Maurel et al., 2010; Tahmasbian et al., 2017). The Aryl1 was
369
also predicted using ANN with the RPD of 2.10 which were considered as ‘highly-reliable’
370
(Fig. 4b). The model was ‘highly-reliable’ when the calculated RPD for the data predicted by
371
the model was above 2 (Bellon-Maurel et al., 2010).
372
The developed PLSR models also showed a reliable prediction of Aryl2, diOAlk1, diOAlk2,
373
Alk, ONAlk and Carbox (Fig. 5-6). Despite the fact that ANN showed a reliable prediction of
374
Aryl2, diOAlk1, diOAlk2 and ONAlk, the accuracies of the ANN models were lower than those
375
obtained from PLSR (Fig. 5-6). The ANN was not successful for predicting Alk and Carbox
376
(Fig. 6 b,f). Unfortunately, neither PLSR nor ANN models successfully predicted OAryl and
377
Carb (R2t < 0.55 and RPD < 1.4) (Fig. 7). We were unable to rationalise the differences in the
378

18

outcomes achieved in the current study. This is the first paper that used hyperspectral image
379
analysis to predict C functional groups in decomposing litterfall samples and the outcomes
380
could not be compared with other existing literature. Hence, further studies using more
381
samples, different band selection methods and various model development techniques are
382
needed to understand lack of OAryl and Carb prediction using hyperspectral image analysis.
383
The PLSR and ANN models were compared in different spectroscopy and hyperspectral
384
imaging studies reporting different results. Some studies reported better predictions using
385
PLSR (Li et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017) and other studies reported better predictions using ANN
386
(Kuang et al., 2015b; Mouazen et al., 2010). The different results might be due to the different
387
nature of the analysed samples and variables, as well as different transformation functions used
388
in ANN.
389
In the current study, both PLSR and ANN models were tested as models to study available C
390
functional group distributions in decomposing leaf litterfall samples using hyperspectral
391
imaging. Although the ANN model proved less effective prediction than the PLSR model in
392
this study, it must be noted that ANN requires larger number of training data in order for the
393
model to learn successfully. Given the practical limitation of the number of comparative
394
datasets available here (i.e. 13C NMR data), then it would be unsurprising that the refinement
395
of the ANN models for current litterfall study was less successful in comparison to the PLSR
396
methods.
397
The ANN could only be suggested to predict Aryl1 while PLSR predicted Alk, ONAlk,
398
diOAlk1, diOalk2, Aryl1, Aryl2 and Carbox. The results might also indicate that the
399
relationships between most of the C functional groups analysed in this study and their spectral
400
reflectance could be explained by linear equations (The equations are provided in
401
supplementary material Equation S1-S7).
402

4 Conclusion
403
The predictability of C functional group distributions in decomposing litterfall samples using
404
hyperspectral images was examined by developing the PLSR and ANN models. Results
405
showed that the PLSR model could successfully predict seven C functional groups (out of nine)
406
including Aryl-C1, Aryl-C2, di-O-alkyl-C1, di-O-alkyl-C2, Alkyl-C, O,N-alkyl-C and Carboxyl
407
derivatives regions with the R2 and RPD to vary from 0.76 to 0.63 and 1.90 to 1.43, respectively
408
in the test sets. The ANN models could predict five C functional groups in the test set which
409
included Aryl-C1, Aryl-C2, di-O-alkyl-C1, di-O-alkyl-C2 and O,N-alkyl-C regions, with the R2
410
and RPD to vary from 0.82 to 0.62 and 2.10 to 1.52, respectively. In view of R2 and RPD, the
411
PLSR models had better prediction compared to the ANN models (with the exception of the
412
Aryl-C1 region). Neither PLSR nor ANN models predicted O-aryl-C and Carbohydrate-C
413
regions successfully. Overall, it was shown that C functional group distributions could be
414
predicted using laboratory-based hyperspectral image analysis and PLSR regression.
